If $\langle a_n\rangle$ is invertible, denote its inverse by $\langle a_n\rangle^{-1}$ (it is unique when it exists, since necessarily $b_1=a_1$ and $b_n=|a_n-a_{n-1}|$); if $\langle a_n\rangle^{-k}$ is invertible, its inverse is $\langle a_n\rangle^{-(k+1)}$ (with $\langle a_n\rangle^0=\langle a_n\rangle$). The sequence is **$k$-invertible** if $\langle a_n\rangle,\langle a_n\rangle^{-1},\dots,\langle a_n\rangle^{-(k-1)}$ are all invertible.

Determine whether there exists a sequence $\langle a_n\rangle$ that is $k$-invertible for all $k\ge1$ (an *infinitely invertible* sequence).
arml-2015-power-08c.answer: No: repeated ruffling forces the terms $a_r^{(-k)}$ eventually below $a_1-(r-2)$ for every $r$, which is impossible for positive integers.
